2.1 SINGLE LINE DIAGRAM
The single line diagram represents the HT and LT electrical power
distribution system of the facility. The incoming 11 kV supply is received from the
utility through the HT metering and protection arrangement, including 11 kV
isolator, H.G. fuse and lightning arresters. The incoming HT supply is connected to a
1000 kVA, 11 kV/433 V transformer, which steps down the voltage to the LT level
for distribution.
The transformer output is connected to the Main MV/LT Panel through a
bus-duct arrangement and an ACB incomer. The main panel distributes power
through multiple outgoing feeders to various loads and sub-distribution boards. The
diagram indicates three major sub-boards, namely SB-1, SB-2 and SB-3, which
supply different electrical loads within the facility.
The diagram also shows three DG sets for standby power generation. DG
Generator-1 is rated at 140 kVA, while DG Generator-3 is rated at 625 kVA; the
third DG set is also integrated into the standby power distribution system. The DG
outputs are connected through dedicated control/protection panels and a DGCO
panel, incorporating ACBs and outgoing feeders for supplying essential loads during
interruption of the utility supply.
The major protection and switching equipment shown in the diagram
includes ACBs, MCCBs, H.G. fuses, load-break switches, CTs and protection relays.
The single line diagram therefore provides an overall representation of the HT
incoming supply, transformer, main distribution panel, DG power sources, sub-
distribution boards and outgoing feeders, and serves as an important reference for
assessing the electrical system, loading, losses, protection and energy-saving
opportunities during the energy audit.

3.1 ANALYSIS OF EB ELECTRICITY BILL FOR THE PERIOD
APRIL 2025 TO MARCH 2026
The electricity consumption and billing pattern of the facility was
analyzed for a period of one year from April 2025 to March 2026 based on the
monthly HT electricity bills. The analysis includes the billed demand, power factor,
demand charges, energy charges, taxes, recorded maximum demand, and monthly
energy consumption.
During the study period, the total electricity consumption was
approximately 5,79,998 kWh, with an average monthly consumption of
approximately 48,333 kWh. The annual net electricity bill amounted to
approximately ₹82.77 lakh, corresponding to an average monthly electricity
expenditure of about ₹6.90 lakh.
The monthly electricity bill varied according to the connected load
utilization and energy consumption. The highest monthly bill was recorded in
September 2025, amounting to approximately ₹8.05 lakh, with an energy
consumption of 61,848 kWh. The lowest monthly bill during the selected period was
recorded in December 2025, at approximately ₹5.80 lakh, corresponding to a
consumption of 34,838 kWh.
The recorded maximum demand varied from 121.2 kVA to 288 kVA
during the year. The highest recorded demand of 288 kVA occurred in August 2025,
while the lowest demand of 121.2 kVA was recorded in December 2025. The
sanctioned/considered 90% demand shown in the bill was 450 kVA. Since the
recorded maximum demand remained below this level throughout the year, no excess
maximum-demand charge was incurred during the study period.
The power factor varied between 0.90 and 0.96. The highest power factor
of 0.96 was recorded in September 2025, while the lowest value of 0.89 occurred in
June 2026. Maintaining the power factor close to unity is important because

CHAPTER 4
ELECTRICAL ENERGY SYSTEM AUDIT AND
PERFORMANCE ASSESSMENT
This chapter presents the performance assessment of the major electrical
systems in the college, including the distribution transformer, Diesel Generator (DG)
set, and Automatic Power Factor Correction (APFC) system. Electrical parameters
were measured using a Fluke Power Quality Analyzer (PQA) and analyzed to
evaluate loading, power factor, energy consumption, losses, and overall system
performance. The results are used to identify energy-saving opportunities and
measures for improving the efficiency and utilization of the electrical system.
4.1 TRANSFORMER PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS
The transformer energy audit was carried out to assess the electrical
performance, loading condition, and energy-efficiency characteristics of the 1000
kVA, 11 kV/433 V distribution transformer installed in the college. The analysis
involved the measurement of important operating parameters such as three-phase
RMS voltage, load current, and apparent power at the transformer output. Voltage
measurements were recorded for the RY, YB, and BR phases to evaluate the voltage
balance and stability of the low-voltage supply system.
The measured phase voltages were found to be approximately 402–404
V, indicating that the transformer is operating with a reasonably stable three-phase
output voltage. Load-current measurements were also obtained for all three phases to
determine the actual electrical demand and to identify any significant phase-wise
load imbalance. The transformer loading analysis was further compared with the
optimum loading condition, considering the relationship between no-load/core losses
and load-dependent copper losses.
Based on the measured losses, the calculated optimum loading was
approximately 38.7% of the transformer rated capacity, corresponding to about 387
kVA for a 1000 kVA transformer.

4.2.1.1 Model Calculation
To clarify the logging process, here is the exact step-by-step
mathematical model applied using the data from April 2025 (Row 3):
Step 1: Total Units Generated (kWh)
Formula: Raw Meter Difference × Multiplier Factor (MF)

Step 2: Generation Cost Per Unit (Rs / kWh)
Formula: Monthly Fuel Expenditure ÷ Total Generated kWh
Calculation: ₹40,936 ÷ 1,140 kWh = ₹35.91 per kWh
Step 3: Specific Energy Consumption (SEC)
Formula: Diesel Consumed (Liters) ÷ Total Generated kWh
Calculation: 430 Liters ÷ 1,140 kWh = 0.38 Liters/kWh
